sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Apart from the pictures, do the type, colours, and shapes share one mood and era, so the piece reads as one whole rather than a collage?** No. The heading (about x 120–593, y 68–104) is a plain, modern bold sans that looks like a utility web page. All three body paragraphs (about x 120–805, y 140–525) are set in a heavy, casual brush script that looks like a café chalkboard or party flyer. The two type voices share nothing except colour. The viewer feels the page was put together from two sources, and the script's festive tone undercuts the practical information it carries: departure intervals, crossing times, bike rules, and the winter cut-off "before dusk." The script also slows reading of the details a passenger acts on. That is a legibility point for the Text section, but it adds to the cost here. Why: the parts share no visible trait, so the page does not read as one thing. The catalog's sources are off the approved list, so this is argued as taste and common sense. Fix: give the page one voice. Set the body in a plain text face that matches the heading, or in a neutral serif paired on purpose with it. If the brand wants personality, keep any script to one short display element, never the running text. Mark: taste (with a defect side: it slows reading of practical information). Weight: major.

**What's working.** The heading names the audience and the topic in plain words ("Notes for ferry passengers"), so a first-time viewer knows at once what the page is and whether it's for them. The copy is finished and tightly organised, with one topic per paragraph (route and timing, bicycles, winter), and it has nothing extra: no ornament, rules, or boxes that need to earn their place.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 7 yes, 1 no (type, colours, and shapes share one mood and era), 0 unsure

**Section.** What matters first: applies. It's a one-screen text notice (1280 × 800) with a title and three body paragraphs.

**Findings**
None.

All three lines come out yes. The heavy script body does make the title's lead narrower than it should be. The bold sans title ("Notes for ferry passengers", about x 120–595, y 68–105) is about 36 px. The body (y 140–520) looks like about 24 px, set in a bold brush script, and its three paragraphs form dark, textured blocks with more total mass than the title. The title still wins on size and comes first, though, and "One element dominates" fails only when elements tie in size and weight. So there's no defect here. The real cost of the script is slow reading of times and rules: a display script used as body text. That belongs to the Text section, so the director should look for it there rather than file it under this one.

**What's working.**
- There are two levels, and they are clearly different: title against body, about 36 vs 24 px. No size is close enough to another to blur which is which.
- The title differs from the body in form as well as size (upright geometric sans against connected script), so it can't be confused with a paragraph even at a glance.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

Walk (working notes): image is 1280×800, about one screen, so I judged it whole. Bash is denied, so I could not run the crop script. First read: the eye lands on the bold sans heading at top left, then drops into three script-face paragraphs in one column at x≈120–805. The right ~475 px and bottom ~280 px are empty. Assumed job: a short web info page for ferry passengers.

1. One grid: yes, single column, every block's left edge is at x≈120.
2. Exact alignment, no near-misses: yes, heading and all paragraphs share x≈120.
3. Baselines across columns: yes, there is only one column.
4. Smaller space inside groups than between them: yes. Paragraph gaps (~55 px baseline to baseline vs ~35 px leading) separate them, and the heading sits with the body it introduces.
5. Boxes hold one group: yes, there are no boxes.
6. No accidental groups: yes.
7. No overlap or touching: yes, at block level. Script ascenders and descenders crowding between lines is a leading question for Text.
8. Margin from page edge: yes, 120 px left and ~65 px top.
9. White space gathered: yes, into one L-shaped field to the right and below.
10. Balance: yes. A left-anchored reading column with open space to the right is the normal web document form and doesn't look like it's tipping.
11. Centering by reason: yes, nothing is centred.
12. One proportion: yes. A single column at a reading-width maximum is the right division here.
13. Eye path: yes, top to bottom, with nothing leading the eye off the page.

No line came out no or unsure, so I opened no entries.

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- Every block hangs from one left edge at x≈120. With a single column and nothing competing, the reader drops straight from the heading through all three paragraphs without hunting for where the next block starts.
- The empty space is in one place: a single field to the right and below the column, not small gaps scattered around the page. The paragraph gaps are clearly bigger than the line spacing, so the three topics (route and timing, bicycles, winter) read as separate notes.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 13 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

sections.report:
**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Is paragraph text set upright in a plain face made for reading, not in italic, underline, script, blackletter, or a display face?** No. All three body paragraphs (about x 120–805, y 140–525, around 24 px) are set in a heavy, slanted brush script. These are practical notes about a timetable, the times crossings take, bike rules and where to find timetables. The reader has to decode each word, because the script's letterforms join, slant and swell. Spots where you have to look twice include "twelve minutes", the joined "ff"/"ft" in "after foot", and "thins to one boat each hour". Reading slows down. Skimming for the facts the text is there to give (every forty minutes, about twelve minutes, last crossing before dusk) gets much harder. The face also hurts readers with low vision or dyslexia more than anyone else. The bold grotesque heading above it ("Notes for ferry passengers", y≈68–105) is plain and confident, which makes the change to script look like an accident rather than a choice. Bringhurst, *The Elements of Typographic Style* 6.2.1, says a text face is "unlikely to be carrying excess ornament". That passage covers faces for text in general and does not name script, so the rule is only partly sourced. Fix: set the paragraphs in a face made for reading, such as a text weight of the heading's own sans or a plain serif. If the piece needs a handmade touch, keep the script for a few words of display at most, never for running text. Defect. Weight: major.

**What's working.** 
- The measure and the paragraph breaks are right for the job. Lines run about 70–75 characters, flush left with a gentle rag. The text is split into three short paragraphs, one topic each (schedule, bicycles, winter), marked by space alone. Once the face is changed, the setting needs no other change.
- The text is near-black on white with no background behind it, so it is high contrast everywhere and the problem is the letterforms alone.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (paragraphs in a plain reading face), 0 unsure

**Section.** Color: applies. The page is near-black text on a white field, with no hues at all.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
1. **The value range is clear.** The heading and body are the same dark charcoal (it looks like a slightly cool near-black, not pure #000), set on plain white. That is close to the strongest light-dark contrast there is. The page would look the same in grayscale, so everything that sets the levels apart has to come from type size, weight and spacing, and that is the right place for it on a text-only page.
2. **The palette is kept to one neutral.** The heading (x≈120–594, y≈68–104) and the three paragraphs (y≈140–520) all use that same ink, so nothing on the page needs to match a second colour. With no colour signals, the reader is never left wondering whether a colour means something. The page's real problems are not about colour: the script face in the body and the empty right half belong to the text and arrangement critics.

**Checklist.** Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure.
